body:
A changing society in the 6th century BCE

The growth of agriculture, towns and commerce changed the organization of society. People increasingly performed different economic roles, and distinctions in wealth and access to resources became more visible.

Society included rulers, priests, cultivators, merchants, artisans, herders, landless workers and other occupational groups.

Some households controlled extensive agricultural resources, while others depended on working for landowners. Wealthy merchants and prosperous householders also became important participants in economic and social life.

Gahapatis and merchants

The term gahapati, related to the Sanskrit grihapati, generally referred to the head or master of a household. In early texts it could also describe a substantial property holder or a prosperous householder.

Some gahapatis controlled land, livestock and labour. Wealthy householders and merchants could provide economic support to religious teachers and communities.

The term should not be interpreted as meaning only a merchant. Its central meaning was connected with household authority and the possession of resources.

Wealthy merchants, sometimes described by terms such as setthi or shreshthin, gained importance through the expansion of trade and urban markets.

The varna order and social distinctions

Later Vedic Brahmanical traditions described society in terms of four varnas:

  • Brahmins: Associated with religious learning and the performance of sacrifices.
  • Kshatriyas: Associated with political authority, protection and warfare.
  • Vaishyas: Associated with agriculture, animal husbandry and trade.
  • Shudras: Assigned service-related functions within the normative varna scheme.

Brahmanical texts often connected varna with birth and prescribed different rights and duties for the groups. However, these prescriptions should not be mistaken for a uniform description of how every community actually lived.

Some thinkers questioned hereditary distinctions, ritual authority and the belief that sacrifices were the only or most important means of achieving religious goals.

Why did new religious movements attract followers?

The 6th–5th centuries BCE witnessed important developments in religious and philosophical thought. Gautama Buddha and Vardhamana Mahavira were among the influential teachers associated with this changing environment.

Both belonged to the broader tradition of renunciation and religious inquiry commonly described as the shramana tradition.

Several conditions helped create an audience for new teachings:

  • Growing towns brought people from different social and occupational backgrounds into contact.
  • Greater commercial wealth allowed merchants and prosperous householders to support religious communities.
  • Questions about social hierarchy, ritual practices, suffering and moral conduct encouraged debate.
  • Travelling teachers could move between villages, towns and political centres, spreading their ideas.

Buddhism and Jainism placed considerable importance on ethical conduct and the actions of individuals. Their teachings offered alternatives to making elaborate Vedic sacrifices central to religious life.

These movements did not arise from economic change alone. They were also part of a wider intellectual and religious environment in which several traditions questioned established ideas.

The relationship with gana-sanghas

The Buddha belonged to the Shakya gana, a clan-based political community. Mahavira was associated with the Licchhavi and Vajji political setting.

The term sangha also came to describe organized communities of Buddhist and Jaina renouncers. However, a religious sangha and a political gana-sangha were different institutions.

A political gana-sangha exercised authority over a territory through a group of ruling members. A religious sangha was an association of monks or nuns organized around religious discipline and teaching.

The importance of patronage

Monks and other renouncers often depended on gifts of food, clothing and shelter. Merchants, landowners, rulers and ordinary followers could provide this support.

The presence of prosperous towns and commercial communities therefore helped sustain religious teachers and their followers.

This explains an important connection: the same economic transformation that supported new political institutions also created opportunities for the development and spread of new religious movements.

Prelims focus

  • Gahapati referred to a householder or household head and could denote a substantial property holder.
  • Wealthy merchants and householders provided support to emerging religious communities.
  • Buddha was associated with the Shakya gana.
  • Mahavira was associated with the Licchhavi-Vajji setting.
  • Buddhism and Jainism developed during the wider social and political changes of the 6th–5th centuries BCE.
  • Trap: A political gana-sangha was not the same institution as a Buddhist or Jaina monastic sangha.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, printed pp. 55–56 and 61–62; Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', printed pp. 65–72; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 38–39; Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', printed pp. 84–86; NIOS, History 315, Lesson 5, printed pp. 63–64, accessed 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Linked economic, social and intellectual changes helped Buddhism and Jainism attract followers; patronage supported them, but no single cause was sufficient.
pictures.caption: Economic and social developments that formed the setting for new religious movements.

title: Social Change and the Background of Jainism and Buddhism

body:
The sixteen important territorial states

During approximately the 6th century BCE, several large territorial states became prominent in northern India and adjoining regions. They are conventionally known as the sixteen mahajanapadas.

The Buddhist text Anguttara Nikaya provides a widely used list of sixteen states. Other early Buddhist and Jaina texts preserve lists that differ in some names. Therefore, the conventional list should be understood as a historically important textual enumeration, not a claim that exactly sixteen political units existed at every moment.

Most of these states were situated in northern India, particularly around the Ganga valley. Others extended into the north-west, central India and the northern Deccan.

Mahajanapadas and their important centres

MahajanapadaCapital or important centreApproximate modern region
AngaChampaEastern Bihar
MagadhaRajagriha; later PataliputraSouthern Bihar
KashiVaranasiVaranasi region, Uttar Pradesh
KosalaShravastiAwadh region, Uttar Pradesh
VajjiVaishaliNorthern Bihar
MallaKusinara and PavaEastern Uttar Pradesh
ChediShuktimati or SotthivatiBundelkhand region
VatsaKaushambiPrayagraj region, Uttar Pradesh
KuruIndraprasthaDelhi, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh
PanchalaAhichchhatra and KampilyaWestern Uttar Pradesh
MatsyaViratanagaraJaipur-Alwar region, Rajasthan
ShurasenaMathuraMathura region, Uttar Pradesh
Assaka or AshmakaPotali or Podana; identifications varyGodavari valley, northern Deccan
AvantiUjjayini and MahishmatiMalwa and Narmada valley, Madhya Pradesh
GandharaTaxilaNorth-western subcontinent, mainly present-day Pakistan
KambojaRajapura is traditionally associated; identification uncertainFar north-western region

Some capitals and place identifications are recorded differently in different historical accounts. For example, Assaka is commonly associated with Potali or Podana, while some textbook tables connect it with Pratishthana or Paithan. Its association with the Godavari region is more secure than the identification of a single capital. Kamboja's capital is likewise not firmly established.

How to understand their distribution

The north-western region

Gandhara and Kamboja occupied the far north-western part of the subcontinent. Taxila was an important centre of Gandhara and connected the region with wider routes of communication and trade.

The western and central Ganga region

Kuru, Panchala, Shurasena, Matsya, Chedi and Vatsa occupied different parts of the northern and central plains and adjoining regions.

Mathura was associated with Shurasena, while Kaushambi was the important centre of Vatsa.

The eastern Ganga region

Kashi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Magadha and Anga were important states in the middle and eastern Ganga region.

Magadha lay principally south of the Ganga, while Vajji was associated with territory north of the river.

Central India and the Deccan

Avanti was an important kingdom in the Malwa region, associated with Ujjayini and Mahishmati.

Assaka or Ashmaka was situated in the Godavari valley. It is particularly important because it is conventionally identified as the only one of the sixteen mahajanapadas located south of the Vindhya region.

Historical maps of the mahajanapadas represent approximate territorial locations. Their boundaries should not be treated as precisely surveyed borders comparable to those of modern administrative units.

The four important competing monarchies

Among the many states, four monarchies became especially prominent in the political struggles of the period:

  • Magadha: Rajagriha, later Pataliputra.
  • Kosala: Shravasti.
  • Vatsa: Kaushambi.
  • Avanti: Ujjayini and Mahishmati.

Magadha eventually emerged as the strongest of these states.

Were any of the sixteen centred in Gujarat?

None of the conventional sixteen mahajanapadas was centred in the territory of present-day Gujarat. The nearest important western political and commercial connections included regions such as Avanti and routes leading towards the western coast.

Gujarat's connection with these developments is therefore mainly through wider patterns of settlement, trade and interaction rather than through a separately listed mahajanapada.

Prelims focus

  • Magadha: Rajagriha; later Pataliputra.
  • Vajji: Vaishali.
  • Vatsa: Kaushambi.
  • Gandhara: Taxila.
  • Avanti: Ujjayini and Mahishmati.
  • Trap: Assaka or Ashmaka belonged to the Godavari region, not the Ganga valley.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 29–31, Map 1; NIOS, History 315, Lesson 5, printed pp. 67–68, Table 5.1 and Map 5.1, accessed 17 November 2026; IGNOU, 'Janapadas and the Mahajanapadas', Unit 14, Section 14.7, accessed 17 November 2026; P. Bhaskar Reddy, 'Mahajanapadas–Rise of Magadha–Nandas–Invasion of Alexander', Outlines of Indian History, UGC INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Section 3, accessed 17 November 2026.]

title: The Sixteen Mahajanapadas: Names, Capitals and Geographical Locations

body:
Different political systems among the mahajanapadas

The mahajanapadas did not all follow the same form of government. Some were ruled by individual kings, while others were governed by groups of ruling families or clan leaders.

The 2 important political forms were monarchies and gana-sanghas.

Monarchical government

In a monarchy, the principal political authority was exercised by a king. Kingship was generally hereditary, although succession and political control could also be influenced by conflict and conquest.

A king directed major political and military decisions. He could employ officials to collect taxes, maintain order and administer the territory. Military power, access to resources and the ability to command loyalty strengthened his position.

Examples of important monarchical states included Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.

Gana-sangha government

In a gana-sangha, political authority was shared among several ruling members rather than concentrated in a single hereditary monarch.

The term gana means a group consisting of several members, while sangha means an organization or association.

Members of the ruling group could meet in assemblies to discuss matters such as warfare, relations with neighbouring states and other important political decisions.

Some members of these assemblies were themselves called rajas, even though no single individual exercised the kind of authority associated with a monarchical ruler.

These governments are often described as oligarchic republics. An oligarchy is a political system in which authority is exercised by a limited group of people.

Ancient gana-sanghas should not be equated with modern representative democracies. Political participation was restricted mainly to eligible members of ruling groups. Women, enslaved people and landless labourers generally did not participate in the political assemblies described in early texts.

Comparison of the two systems

FeatureMonarchyGana-sangha
Principal authorityIndividual kingGroup of ruling members
Political successionGenerally hereditaryBased on membership and practices of ruling groups
Important decisionsDirected by the king and his advisersDiscussed by assemblies of ruling members
Political participationConcentrated in the royal establishmentRestricted to eligible members of ruling groups
ExamplesMagadha, Kosala, Vatsa, AvantiVajji, Malla

Vajji: an important gana-sangha

Vajji, also called Vrijji, was an important confederacy in northern Bihar. Its principal political centre was Vaishali.

The Licchhavis were an important constituent group of the Vajji confederacy. The political organization included several ruling members who participated in collective deliberation.

Because authority was shared among ruling groups, the political structure of Vajji differed from the monarchical system of Magadha.

Vajji nevertheless had territory, political institutions and military interests. It could therefore become involved in conflicts with neighbouring monarchies.

Malla and other gana traditions

Malla was another important example of a gana-sangha. It was associated with the centres of Kusinara and Pava in the eastern Uttar Pradesh region.

Other smaller clan-based political communities included the Shakyas, among whom the Buddha was born.

The Shakya gana was a smaller political community and should not be confused with a separate entry in the conventional list of sixteen mahajanapadas.

Why the distinction matters

Both monarchies and gana-sanghas were territorial political organizations, but they differed in how authority was distributed.

The central distinction is not whether an ancient polity had a city, an army or influential leaders. It is whether political power was concentrated in one king or shared among a limited group of ruling members.

Prelims focus

  • Magadha was an important monarchy.
  • Vajji was an important gana-sangha centred at Vaishali.
  • The Licchhavis were associated with the Vajji confederacy.
  • Malla was associated with Kusinara and Pava.
  • Members of the ruling group in a gana-sangha could collectively be called rajas.
  • Trap: Ancient gana-sanghas did not provide universal political participation.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, 'Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic', printed pp. 60–62; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 29–30; NIOS, History 315, Lesson 5, printed pp. 67–68, accessed 17 November 2026; P. Bhaskar Reddy, Outlines of Indian History, Chapter 8, Sections 3.4–3.5, UGC INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, accessed 17 November 2026.]

title: Monarchies and Gana-Sanghas: Two Forms of Political Government
